title: Four-high replaceable memory bricks in a 2D array
idea: MINIFY the repair unit: instead of 12- to 16-high stacks, use many 4-high bricks tiled flat on the substrate, each individually removable, so a failure costs one small brick.
why: HBM yield (stack yield compounds per die) and repair cost: claims ~2x better stack yield and cheap field swaps.

title: Na: sodium-silicate geopolymer encapsulant replaces epoxy around HBM stacks
idea: Fill and encapsulate HBM stacks with a low-temperature (~80 C cure) sodium-silicate aluminosilicate geopolymer loaded with AlN, giving an inorganic mold with CTE ~6-8 ppm/K, ~3-5 W/m-K and no outgassing; package outline and ballout stay unchanged.
why: Thermal and warpage (facts 3, 6): ~5-10x the conductivity of epoxy mold underfill lowers stack temperature and warpage, enabling taller stacks from abundant Na, Al, Si.

title: Train-timetable DRAM: compiler-scheduled interface without command bus
idea: Railways run on timetables, not per-trip dispatch. The AI compiler pre-loads a deterministic access schedule (row, bank, cycle) into a small sequencer on the HBM base die. The sequencer opens rows just in time and streams data in fixed slots. The host sends only a start token and occasional amendments.
why: Drops command/address pins and most controller handshakes. That frees bumps for data (~10-15% more bandwidth per stack) and wastes fewer activations, because each row opens exactly when it is needed.

title: MicroLED mass-transfer stamps tile micro-chiplet DRAM in laminated layers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Dice DRAM into 0.5 mm micro-chiplets and use microLED elastomer stamps to place 1e4 per stroke into a planarized polymer layer with printed RDL, repeating 10-20 layers like a PCB build-up.
why: Tiny chiplets yield ~99% and reclaim wafer-edge area, mass transfer cuts placement cost ~100x, and the layered build gives ~10x bits per footprint.

title: Ant pheromone: hot pages migrate autonomously toward requesting chiplet
idea: Like ants following pheromone trails: each memory chiplet keeps per-page counters tagged by requester, and pages whose trail strength crosses a threshold migrate across the chiplet mesh toward the heaviest user in the background.
why: Data-movement energy: 30-40% fewer mesh hops on average for multi-chiplet accelerators.

title: Bookshelf stack: dies stand on edge in an etched rack
idea: Rotate the stack 90 degrees: thin dies are diced, given sidewall pads by angled shadow-mask evaporation over the edge, and inserted vertically into a DRIE-etched silicon rack whose trench floors carry solder pads, so every die connects straight to the base with no TSVs and no die-to-die relay.
why: TSV tax eliminated (fact 6): each die gets its own edge bus (hundreds of I/O at 20 um pitch), and dies cool from both faces with fluid flowing between them.

title: Electrohydrodynamic-printed copper pillars replace bumping lines
idea: Substitute photolithographic bumping and plating with electrohydrodynamic direct printing of 5-10 um copper micro-pillars voxel by voxel onto die pads, so one desktop printer turns bare purchased dies into fine-pitch flip-chip parts.
why: Capital intensity: replaces a ~$50M bumping line for low-volume memory-on-logic assemblies.

title: Wood nanocellulose paper interposer with silicon-matched thermal expansion
idea: The interposer core is transparent cellulose-nanofiber 'nanopaper' (CTE ~3-8 ppm/K, close to silicon), which copies the low-expansion fibril architecture of plant cell walls. It is made from wood pulp on roll-to-roll paper lines, laminated with a moisture barrier and metallized with semi-additive copper RDL.
why: Scarce resources and capital intensity: wood-derived and roll-to-roll, so it avoids the quartz-crucible and silicon-wafer chains for interposers and taps large U.S. pulp capacity.

title: Ag: maskless inkjet-silver RDL for low-volume memory interposers
idea: Print redistribution layers with nano-silver ink sintered at ~150 C and inkjet-printed polyimide dielectric directly on glass or organic interposers at 5-10 um lines, so custom memory-chiplet interposers need no photomasks, steppers or plating lines.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): removes ~$100k-1M mask sets per interposer design and litho tools; lets small U.S. firms build HBM-style packages in weeks.

title: Spheroidality: ring of compute chiplets with memory inside and outside
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality (curves instead of lines): place compute chiplets in a ring on a large panel substrate, giving the ring both an inner and an outer shoreline. Memory stacks sit inside the hole and around the outside.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~1.6x more memory beachfront per unit of compute area at the same short wire length, avoiding longer links with higher pJ/bit.

title: Endoscope imaging-fiber bundle carries 10,000 slow microLED memory lanes
idea: Medical endoscopes pipe whole images through coherent bundles of ~10k fiber cores. Couple a microLED array on the memory module to a photodiode array on the processor through an imaging fiber bundle, each pixel-lane at ~1-2 Gb/s with no SerDes, DSP or lasers.
why: Off-board memory links at ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit vs DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit (>10x), so cheap DRAM can sit meters away in pooled racks; avoids laser and EUV scarcity.

title: Submariner's sonar: GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded stack
idea: Sound travels well through solids: put ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses vertically through the bonded stack as a contactless data bus, with frequency-division channels assigned per die.
why: TSV-free vertical signalling with no drilled vias, which recovers the TSV area tax and yield loss; speculative 10-50 Gb/s per transducer site at sub-pJ energy.

title: Sub-terahertz plastic waveguide ribbons replace DDR copper channels
idea: Substitute PCB DDR traces with PTFE/HDPE dielectric ribbon waveguides carrying 140-300 GHz carriers from CMOS transceivers in the memory controller to modules up to 1 m away; each ribbon moves 50-100 Gb/s with no equalization and no connector stubs.
why: Fact 5: DDR5 10-20 pJ/bit to ~2-3 pJ/bit; distance freedom enables rack-scale pooled DRAM, recovering the ~20-30% stranded memory.

title: Die-level erasure coding admits cheap downbinned dies into 48-high stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Spread every cache line Reed-Solomon coded across 40 data dies plus 8 parity dies, with the base die mapping out dead banks, so dies with failed banks or weak cells (today scrapped or sold at 40-60% off) become first-class stack members.
why: Stack yield stops multiplying and discounted partial-good dies pay for the extra tiers: ~10x bits per package at the same package price.

title: Array-only DRAM sensed directly by the processor's sense amplifiers
idea: Eliminate the memory die's periphery and PHY: the DRAM die carries only cells, local bitlines and wordline stubs; every 32-bitline group feeds a local charge-transfer pre-amp to one ~1 um hybrid-bond pad, and the sense amps, decoders and row buffers live in the logic die beneath on fast low-voltage transistors. The 'interface' is a bitline.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and IO is 3-4 pJ/bit: removing both gives ~1.8-2x bits per DRAM wafer, puts the row buffer next to compute and drops movement to ~0.1 pJ/bit.

title: Firefly-lantern microLED arrays on sapphire for wide-and-slow memory optics
idea: Fireflies get light out efficiently through a nanostructured cuticle. GaN microLEDs grown on sapphire get firefly-like tapered light-extraction structures and are bonded to glass interposers, where they drive hundreds of parallel 2-5 Gb/s fiber-bundle or waveguide channels to memory with no lasers.
why: Interface energy and reach (fact 5): ~0.3-1 pJ/bit at meter reach for pooled memory racks, using mature GaN-on-sapphire lines outside silicon fabs.

title: Nacre brick-and-mortar ceramic substrate for large memory packages
idea: The silicon interposer is replaced with a nacre-mimetic laminate of aligned alumina or glass microplatelets in a thin polymer 'mortar', made by freeze-casting or tape casting. Its CTE is tuned to ~4-6 ppm/K, it is stiff and crack-arresting, and fine RDL is built on top at panel scale.
why: Capital intensity and package size: allows >100 cm^2 packages with 12-16 memory stacks without silicon interposer stitching or warpage failure; substrate cost per area ~5x below silicon.

title: Diamond interlayers let DRAM sit directly on the hot GPU
idea: Invert 'memory must sit beside the hot compute die': bond thin single-crystal diamond plates grown in Washington state between GPU and stacked DRAM to spread heat sideways, with through-diamond vias carrying signals.
why: Diamond's ~2000 W/m-K lets memory go on top of logic without overheating: face-to-face 3D bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit and no interposer.

title: Japanese swordsmith's folded steel: nanotwinned copper TSVs and bonds
idea: Folded steel is tough because of its layering: plate all TSVs, pillars and hybrid-bond pads as (111) nanotwinned copper, whose twin boundaries block vacancy flow and allow 150-200 C direct bonding.
why: Electromigration life about 10x that of normal Cu at 125 C, and lower bonding temperature limits DRAM retention damage during assembly; this enables 125 C/10 year stacks.

title: Micro-coax wire bonds bring 50 Gb/s to cheap stacks
idea: Substitute TSVs in wide-IO stacks with standard gold wire bonds that are parylene-coated and then sputtered with a grounded metal shell, turning each into a 50-ohm micro-coax; staircase-stacked LPDDR dies get impedance-controlled vertical lanes from a used wire bonder and a parylene coater.
why: Fact 6: no TSV tax; per-wire rate rises from ~6 to 25-50 Gb/s, letting wire-bonded stacks approach HBM bandwidth at a fraction of the cost.

title: Layer-clocked just-in-time weight streaming caps HBM at 4 GB
idea: Scarcity: each accelerator gets only 4 GB of local DRAM. Since transformer layer order is deterministic, the compiler emits an exact transfer schedule so layer L+2's weights and KV blocks land from pooled far memory into a double-buffered ring exactly as layer L finishes.
why: Does DRAM's job with less: local HBM per accelerator drops 5-20x and far memory can be cheaper DDR/LPDDR, sidestepping HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit (fact 6).

title: Clockless delay-insensitive links inside the HBM stack
idea: Po: time is abolished. Replace the stack's source-synchronous DDR interface with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive asynchronous encoding on TSVs and microbumps, deleting DLLs, PLLs and link training so lanes idle at zero power and run as fast as voltage and temperature allow.
why: Shrinks PHY periphery and idle power and enables deep voltage scaling; ~30% interface energy cut.

title: Address-free scheduled-stream DRAM programmed at compile time
idea: Shift address generation from runtime nanoseconds to compile time: for AI graphs the whole access sequence is known, so the compiler loads a compact access program into the stack's base die, which streams rows in order with no command/address traffic. The host simply consumes a tape.
why: Eliminates command/address bus pins and energy and lets each row be activated once and fully consumed, attacking 128x overfetch (fact 8) and bus energy (fact 5): ~20-30% interface energy saved.

title: Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion: programmable roller stamps transfer only known-good DRAM dies
idea: A roller stamp with an addressable electrode array energizes Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion only under dies that passed wafer test, lifting thousands of known-good DRAM chiplets per revolution and printing them onto a moving interposer web.
why: Assembly throughput and yield (fact 6): massively parallel known-good-die transfer with no pick-and-place capex.

title: Wafer-scale memory carpet replaces stacked HBM
idea: MAGNIFY the interposer to a full 300 mm passive silicon wafer and MINIFY stack height to one: ~200 single DRAM dies tile the wafer flat around ~20 accelerator dies, so every die is within ~5 mm of compute and needs no TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): uses DDR-cost dies at HBM-class bandwidth; claims ~2-3x lower cost per GB/s.

title: Drum-memory revival: command-free rotational streaming mode for HBM stacks
idea: Add a 'drum mode' in which each bank activates rows in a fixed cyclic order and streams them past the PHY like drum tracks past fixed heads, with no command/address traffic; a compiler places tensors at rotational offsets (IBM 650 SOAP-style optimum programming) so data arrives exactly when compute needs it.
why: Facts 3/7/8: drops C/A pins and scheduler logic (~15-20% of PHY area/power), every opened row is fully consumed (no 128x overfetch) for streaming AI loads, and refresh becomes implicit because every row is read once per rotation inside the retention window.

title: Vacuum-gap floating electrodes in hermetic cavities hold charge for years
idea: Ideal: a capacitor with no leakage path at all. Closest achievable: each cell is a micro-electrode suspended in a wafer-level vacuum cavity with no dielectric to tunnel through, charged by a field-emission tip on write and sensed capacitively by an underlying transistor gate without contact, so stored charge persists for years without refresh.
why: Facts 1 and 3: removes both the dielectric and junction leakage paths that force refresh; hermetic vacuum packaging becomes the memory technology itself.

title: Sun proximity-communication revival: capacitive face-to-face HBM with no bumps
idea: Revive Sun Microsystems' abandoned proximity communication: memory and logic dies overlap face-to-face with 10-20 um pads coupled capacitively across a 1-3 um plain SiO2 gap, clamped mechanically, with electronic pad steering cancelling misalignment.
why: Constraint: no underfill, fluoropolymer adhesive, plating or fluorinated etch; dies stay reworkable so known-good stacks replace bad ones (fact 6 yield), at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit and 10k+ channels/mm^2.

title: Shingled-roof staircase stack with aerosol-printed silver wires
idea: Offset dies like roof shingles so each die's pad row is exposed on a staircase. Then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the steps and sinter them at ~200 C, replacing both TSVs and wirebonds.
why: TSV-free stacking at low capex. Printed 10-20 um lines give far more connections than wirebonds and avoid TSV yield loss, which suits capacity-tier memory.

title: Twin synchronized predictors send only the surprise
idea: Information theory says only unpredicted bits must cross a channel. Run identical stride/context/value predictors on both sides of the memory link; the sender transmits a 1-bit hit flag when the receiver's prediction is right and an XOR residual otherwise, and both update identically so they stay in lockstep.
why: Regular pointers, zeros and strides could cut bits crossing the interface 2-5x, lowering link pJ and bandwidth demand (facts 5, 8).

title: Computational sprinting's wax died; salt-hydrate buffers let HBM burst bandwidth
idea: Computational sprinting (UPenn, 2012) proposed paraffin heat buffers but never shipped because wax conducts poorly and re-solidifies slowly. Fill the spacer and dummy-die volumes beside HBM stacks with magnesium nitrate hexahydrate (melts ~89 C, ~160 J/g) infiltrated into sealed copper foam, which soaks up heat right at HBM's throttle point so stacks can run 20-40% higher bandwidth for tens of seconds and re-freeze during idle phases.
why: Thermal throttling and temperature-doubled refresh (fact 3) during AI bursts, letting a smaller memory system meet peak demand; Mg, N, O, H and Cu only.

title: DRAM-bridge: the chiplet bridge die is itself memory
idea: Rearrange the bridge's role: the small embedded silicon bridges (EMIB/LSI-style) that link adjacent GPU chiplets are fabricated as DRAM dies whose top metals carry the die-to-die wires and whose array area is dual-ported to both neighbouring chiplets' edge bumps. Silicon that today only carries wires becomes a shared buffer between neighbours.
why: A 16 mm2 bridge at ~0.3 Gb/mm2 holds ~0.6 GB, so 8 bridges add ~5 GB of on-package shared memory at <0.5 pJ/bit with zero extra package area; chiplets exchange tensors through memory instead of the link (fact 5).

title: Spectrum-sliced LED WDM failed in telecom; incandescent silicon sources suit packages
idea: Spectrum-sliced incoherent WDM (one broadband source cut into channels) died in telecom from excess intensity noise and low power per slice over km distances. Over 1-10 mm in-package paths, a microheated SiC/silicon photonic-crystal selective thermal emitter (W-free) can feed SiN waveguides whose silicon microrings slice and modulate dozens of channels, detected by Si photodiodes below 1.1 um, with no laser at all.
why: Removes III-V lasers (Ga, In), the dominant cost and failure item in co-packaged optics, from memory links; ~5 pJ/bit at first with a path toward ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Farmer's crop rotation: supply TSVs swap VDD and VSS roles
idea: A farmer rotates crops so soil recovers: on-die power switches periodically swap which TSV groups carry VDD and which carry VSS, reversing the DC current direction in each via every few hours so electromigration damage partly heals.
why: Electromigration life falls about 4x from 105 C to 125 C; bipolar stress can extend via life by about 5-10x, so power TSVs can be smaller or fewer at 125 C (less TSV area).

title: Sun Proximity Communication fixed by capillary self-alignment and electronic pad steering
idea: Sun's capacitive face-to-face proximity communication died because overlapping chips needed micron-level alignment and gap control that packaging could not hold. Place DRAM tiles over logic tiles by water-droplet capillary self-assembly (hydrophilic landing sites give <1 um placement), set the gap with oxide standoffs, and oversample each signal with a 3x3 cluster of transmit micro-pads from which the receiver picks the best-aligned one at boot: no solder, no TSVs, reworkable tiles.
why: Data movement and the HBM TSV tax: ~0.1 pJ/bit capacitive links at 10-20 um pitch with no bonding yield loss; reworkable tiles remove stack-yield multiplication (fact 6, 20-30% loss).

title: Bookshelf DRAM: dies standing on edge in slotted carriers
idea: Substitute vertical stacking with edge mounting: dies with pads redistributed to one edge stand upright in a laser-machined or 3D-printed ceramic slotted carrier, like books, with each edge soldered to substrate pads at 50 um pitch; ~50 dies per cm of shelf.
why: Near-HBM density per footprint without TSVs or thinning, and each die is independently reworkable so stack-yield coupling (Fact 6) disappears.

title: Melting-point depression: low-temperature sintered copper nanoink printed redistribution layers
idea: Inkjet/EHD-print 3-5 um Cu nanoparticle lines whose size-depressed melting point lets them sinter below 200 C under photonic flash, forming fan-out RDL on molded memory panels without lithography, sputter or plating tools.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): replaces litho+plating for fan-out lines; no silver; low thermal budget protects retention; 2-3x bulk resistivity is acceptable for fan-out.

title: Electric-fish jamming avoidance for in-package wireless memory links
idea: Each DRAM tier and the base die carry tiny near-field coils. Like electric fish shifting their discharge frequency away from neighbours, each link autonomously moves its carrier to avoid interference, so many vertical and lateral wireless channels share the package without static frequency planning.
why: TSV cost and yield (fact 6): wireless vertical links free dies from TSVs and allow dies from different vendors and nodes to be mixed in one stack.

title: Gecko-setae dry adhesion for reworkable, repairable memory stacks
idea: Dies in a stack are held by gecko-like micro-pillar dry adhesive with spring-contact or liquid-metal interconnect pads, instead of permanent hybrid bonds and underfill. A stack that fails final test can be peeled apart and only the bad die swapped.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): today one bad die scraps an 8-16-die stack; repairability could recover most of the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: Ca: calcium-gettered vacuum-gap interposer wiring with k equal to one
idea: Etch away the inter-line dielectric of interposer RDL to leave Cu lines suspended on posts, seal the package hermetically, and hold the gaps at high vacuum with an evaporated calcium getter film, giving k~1.0 and zero dielectric loss between memory lines.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~3-4x lower line capacitance than SiO2, interposer/HBM I/O energy down ~60% and higher bandwidth per mm of die edge.

title: Telephone-hybrid revival: simultaneous bidirectional signaling doubles every TSV
idea: Revive the telephone 2-wire/4-wire hybrid and Edison's quadruplex telegraph: each TSV and microbump carries read and write data at once, and an on-die replica-driver hybrid subtracts the local transmit waveform from the received sum.
why: Fact 6: halves TSV/bump count per unit bandwidth (or doubles stack bandwidth), shrinking the TSV area tax that makes HBM ~3x the wafer area per bit; ~10-15% die area back.

title: Diels-Alder reversible underfill that unzips at 120 C
idea: MINIFY rework damage: the underfill is a thermally reversible Diels-Alder polymer network that depolymerizes near 120 C, so microbumped memory dies lift off cleanly and re-underfill afterward.
why: Repairable 2.5D/3D packages; a bad HBM or chiplet is reworked instead of scrapping the whole module.

title: LC resonance: adiabatic energy-recovery memory buses recycle interposer line charge
idea: Make interposer line groups part of resonant LC tanks with on-package thin-film inductors so charge sloshes between line and inductor instead of dumping to ground; data is encoded in the phase/polarity of the resonant swing, resonant clocking applied to data.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and CV^2 floor (fact 10): recovers 60-80% of line energy, HBM bus ~3.5 to ~1 pJ/bit; constrains encoding to near-periodic signaling.

title: Open chiplet memory socket standard to admit new DRAM makers
idea: Substitute vendor-dominated JEDEC HBM interfaces with a CHIPS-funded, royalty-free chiplet memory protocol on UCIe plus open reference base-die IP, so any new U.S. memory die maker can attach to any accelerator without building a full HBM PHY.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes $100M+ of PHY/interface development from a new entrant's path, diversifying supply.

title: Sidewall-printed vertical buses replace TSVs in offset die stacks
idea: Scarcity: TSVs banned. Stack thinned DRAM dies with a 20 um staircase offset so every die exposes an edge pad row, then aerosol-jet print 10 um copper/silver traces down the stepped sidewall (with printed polymer dielectric between traces) to tie every tier to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV-driven 20-30% yield loss, recovering ~25-30% of die area per bit; printing tools are cheap and U.S.-available.

title: Thermophile biologist: fully intermetallic TLP microbumps that cannot age
idea: Thermophilic archaea survive 120 C by using bonds that are already at equilibrium: convert every Cu/Sn microbump completely to Cu3Sn during bonding (transient liquid phase), so no further intermetallic growth or Kirkendall voiding can happen in 10 years at 125 C.
why: Removes the main wear-out mode of memory microbumps at high temperature; lets 25-40 um microbumps survive automotive Grade 0/1 life without hybrid-bonding capex.

title: Optical clock broadcast from above, no clock pins
idea: Reverse forwarded-clock wiring: one modulated LED or laser illuminates the package through a window, and silicon photodiodes on every memory and logic die recover the same clock edge simultaneously, removing clock trees, DLLs and clock bumps from the memory interface.
why: Clocking is ~20-40% of PHY energy; a skew-free global clock shrinks PHY area (fact 7) and link energy (fact 5); photodiodes and windows are simple uni-fab structures.

title: Harvest HBM stacks from retired accelerators onto new boards
idea: Po: dead GPUs are memory mines. Run a laser-assisted debond and reball line that lifts HBM stacks off retired or failed accelerator interposers, re-tests them, and mounts them on a low-cost organic carrier as CXL or inference memory modules.
why: DRAM outlives the 3-4 year accelerator cycle; recycling adds supply with no wafer starts, cutting scarce-resource and capital use per bit.

title: Thrift store: buy fab-reject DRAM dies, remap bad rows in controller
idea: Like a thrift store selling flawed goods: buy partial-good DRAM dies that fail fab repair budgets at scrap prices, package them conventionally, and pair them with a controller (FPGA or CXL ASIC firmware) that holds large per-die bad-row and weak-cell remap tables.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer already produced, perhaps 2-5% more effective supply, at very low cost per bit.

title: Ferreed-switch revival: magnetically latched crosspoints circuit-switch pooled memory
idea: Revive Bell's 1960s ferreed (remanent-magnet-latched reed switch from No. 1 ESS) as MEMS crosspoint arrays with semi-hard magnetic latches that connect any server's copper lanes to any memory sled and hold with zero power.
why: Constraint: glass-sealed NiFe reeds need no fluorinated chemistry or fluoropolymer insulation; circuit switching adds no per-access latency or energy (just a wire) versus 100+ ns and several pJ/bit through CXL packet switches.

title: Bookbinding spine bus: plated sidewall links across die stacks
idea: Stack dies like book pages with routing pulled to their edges, grind the spine flat, and plate and laser-pattern conductors down the spine, like glue binding a book. The whole stack's bus lives on its sidewall.
why: No TSVs in the DRAM die, and works for commodity dies; removes TSV area tax with i-line-class patterning.

title: Wireless mm-wave weight broadcast to many chiplets at once
idea: Eliminate per-consumer copies and point-to-point wires for read-shared data: one memory chiplet broadcasts weight tiles over a 200-300 GHz on-package antenna and waveguide cavity, and 16-64 compute chiplets receive the same bits simultaneously.
why: Parallel inference fetches the same weights N times and replicates them in N local memories; broadcast cuts weight traffic and replicated capacity by ~N.

title: Significance-aware lanes: MSBs robust, LSBs cheap and noisy
idea: Invert 'all bits deserve the same wire': route sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits over full-swing terminated lanes and low-mantissa bits over ultra-low-swing unterminated lanes run at a bit-error rate AI numerics tolerate.
why: Half or more of tensor bits ride at 3-5x lower energy; ~40% lower interface energy for AI traffic.

title: Industrial-longevity harvest-and-rebin of retired server DRAM
idea: Factories keep 30-year-old controllers alive by harvesting parts. Build automated lines that pull DIMMs from retired servers, burn-in and speed-bin them, and repackage the dies into CXL memory expanders for cold/warm tiers sold with a supply guarantee.
why: Hyperscalers retire servers every 4-6 years with DRAM good for 10+; recovering even 30% adds several percent to annual usable supply at a fraction of new-bit cost.

title: Uncut DRAM wafer serves as the interposer for chiplets
idea: An interposer is just wires on silicon, and a DRAM wafer is already silicon with metal. Leave the DRAM wafer uncut, add a top RDL, and hybrid-bond logic chiplets face-down so each sits on its own memory field; boot-time self-test maps out bad dies and routes around them through the wafer RDL.
why: Deletes interposer, dicing, KGD handling and HBM TSVs: wafer-scale bandwidth at <0.2 pJ/bit and ~30-40% lower packaged cost per bit for HBM-class memory (facts 5, 6).

title: MIDI-style memory: ship generator seeds, regenerate data beside DRAM
idea: Adapted from MIDI, which sends notes rather than audio: regenerable tensor parts (random projections, low-rank bases, positional tables) are stored as seeds plus generator code. A 180 nm PRNG/LFSR engine on the memory buffer recreates them on the fly instead of reading them.
why: Data movement and capacity: regenerable tensors are neither stored nor moved; ~10-30% capacity and bandwidth savings for suitable models.

title: Photonic base die: stacks talk to GPUs by fiber
idea: Invert 'the HBM base die is electrical logic beside the GPU': build the base die on a U.S. monolithic silicon-photonics process (GlobalFoundries Fotonix, New York) so all stack I/O leaves as light on fiber and stacks can sit centimeters to meters away.
why: Removes the silicon interposer and its reticle limit on stacks per GPU; ~1-2 pJ/bit with capacity scaling past 8 stacks.

title: Self-healing interposer with GeTe switches rerouting dead bumps
idea: Po: the package rewires itself after it is built. Embed phase-change GeTe RF switches in the interposer routing layer so that, after assembly test, channels are re-routed around open microbumps or bad TSV lanes by pulsing the switches once.
why: HBM assembly yield is down 20-30% and one bad stack can scrap a whole module; post-assembly repair recovers most of that loss.

title: Cray-2 immersion revival with ester fluids enables taller HBM stacks
idea: Revive the Cray-2's total-immersion cooling but swap Fluorinert for natural or synthetic ester dielectric fluid, with micro-jets aimed through the gaps between stacks and a passive thermosiphon loop, removing heat through stack sidewalls.
why: Constraint: no PFAS coolants (Fluorinert/Novec production has been exited); side-cooling relieves the thermal cap on stack height so 16-24-high stacks run unthrottled, ~50% more GB per footprint.

title: High-bandwidth flash stacks feed read-mostly weights through SRAM staging
idea: Worsen: keep weights written once a month in memory built for endless writes. Flip: stack charge-trap NAND dies with many small planes in the HBM footprint, read them wide and in parallel into a base-die SRAM staging buffer, and serve weights from there, leaving DRAM only for KV and activations.
why: Cost per bit: NAND is ~10-20x cheaper per bit than HBM; endurance is irrelevant for weights and deterministic streaming hides flash latency.

title: Pyroelectricity: self-powered per-bank thermal telemetry drives fine-grained refresh
idea: Deposit thin AlScN pyroelectric patches over each DRAM bank in the stack; temperature changes generate charge with no bias, integrated and read via spare sideband lanes, so the controller refreshes each bank at its true temperature instead of the stack worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): most banks run far cooler than the hottest spot; 20-40% fewer refreshes and recovered bandwidth.

title: 1968 ECDM revival: spark-drilled glass interposer vias in caustic, no HF
idea: Revive Kurafuji's electrochemical discharge machining: tool electrodes in NaOH/KOH electrolyte create gas-film sparks that thermally and chemically drill 20-50 um vias through glass interposer panels, with arrays of parallel electrodes for throughput.
why: Constraint: removes hydrofluoric acid (laser-induced deep etching) and SF6 plasma from glass via formation, unlocking large, cheap, low-loss glass panels that host many HBM stacks.

title: Defect-map matchmaking pairs wafers so tall W2W stacks still yield
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Keep a pool of thousands of probed DRAM wafers and run an assignment solver that stacks wafers whose bad die sites coincide (bad-on-bad), so defects concentrate in a few stack columns instead of poisoning many.
why: Wafer-on-wafer yield falls as y^N; matching can lift 32-high stack yield from ~20% to ~60% at typical defect densities, making 10x tiers affordable.

title: Deep-space PPM: one pulse carries four to six bits
idea: NASA's deep-space optical link uses pulse-position modulation because photons are scarce. Encode each 4-6-bit symbol as the position of a single short current pulse within a 16-64-slot frame on each memory lane; one transition per symbol replaces several NRZ transitions, and idle lanes send nothing.
why: Transitions per bit fall ~4-8x; with low-swing pulsed drivers, link energy ~10x below DDR5/HBM PHYs, at the cost of a faster slot clock and tighter timing.

title: Line-rate exponent-sharing and ANS codec inside the base die
idea: Scarcity: no redundant bit may cross the link. The HBM base die carries a block-floating-point repacker (shared exponent per 32 values) plus an asymmetric-numeral-systems entropy coder that losslessly compresses BF16/FP8 tensors at line rate; the GPU memory controller decodes.
why: Data movement (fact 5): BF16 exponents hold ~2.5 bits of entropy in 8, giving 1.3-1.6x effective bandwidth and capacity without touching cells.

title: Trusted-packaging-first US strategy: stack imported wafers domestically
idea: DoD trusted-foundry users secure supply through trusted assembly. Fund US memory OSATs that buy commodity DRAM wafers from several countries and do base-die integration, stacking, test and HBM/CXL module assembly onshore, with tariff exemptions on wafers and offtake from federal AI programs.
why: Packaging capex is ~1/10 of a DRAM fab with a 1-2 year ramp; moves the highest-value, scarcest step (HBM assembly) onshore years before a US fab could.

title: Scatter-gather descriptor port returns only the useful bytes
idea: Worsen: open a whole 1-8 KB row to deliver one 4-byte embedding element. Flip: give the HBM base die a descriptor port where the host posts index lists; the base die activates sub-rows, gathers only the requested sectors into dense packets and ships those, so the bus carries only useful bytes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 4-16x fewer bits moved per useful bit for sparse embedding, graph and MoE routing workloads.

title: Stack untested dies, route around failures with a base-die crossbar
idea: Reverse test-then-stack: stack 14 lightly tested dies for a 12-die product and put a channel crossbar in the base die that maps logical channels onto whichever dies and channels pass final package test, set by fuses. Yield comes from routing around defects rather than from known-good-die screening.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): ~14% die over-provisioning lifts stack yield from ~70% to >95% and removes a costly wafer-level test insertion.

title: Stack-first, test-later: base die remaps around untested dies
idea: Invert 'only known-good dies are stacked': stack lightly tested dies with ~20% spare capacity and let the base die run full BIST after bonding, building a per-subarray remap table that routes around bad rows, banks or whole dies.
why: Removes costly per-die KGD testing and turns HBM's 20-30% stack-yield loss into graceful capacity derating.

title: CVD-diamond interlayers replace silicon spacers in tall stacks
idea: Substitute dummy silicon spacers and mold compound between DRAM dies with 20 um polycrystalline diamond wafers carrying laser-drilled vias, so every bond layer is a lateral heat spreader (k ~1,500 vs ~150 W/mK).
why: Heat limits HBM to 12-16 high: 24-32-high stacks (about 2x GB per stack) at the same junction temperature.

title: Mussel-foot catechol bonding of chiplets onto glass at room temperature
idea: Mussels stick to wet rock with DOPA catechol-metal coordination bonds. Memory chiplets are attached to a glass panel substrate with a catechol-functionalized adhesive that cures near room temperature, filled with conductive particles only over the pads, which avoids the CTE mismatch and warpage of 250-400 C bonding.
why: Packaging yield and cost: low-temperature bonding on glass removes warpage-driven yield loss in large multi-stack packages and the need for silicon interposers, and allows reworkable bonds.

title: Jacquard-loom woven micro-wire substrate with laser-fused crossings
idea: Weave 10 um insulated copper micro-wires (weft = signals) through glass-fiber warp on a Jacquard loom; a punched-card-style program decides which warp/weft crossings get laser-stripped and welded into vias. The result is a multilayer memory-to-compute substrate made with no lithography.
why: Cuts substrate capex and lead time; woven routing gives low-loss round wire (lower pJ/bit than flat traces) and ~10 um pitch without masks.

title: NAND-style zig-zag wire-bond stacks put 64 DRAM dies in one package
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Borrow mobile NAND packaging, where 16-32 dies stack in a zig-zag staircase with wire bonds for cents, and apply it to DRAM as a capacity tier: 64 dies per package on 8 wire-bonded channels at modest bandwidth.
why: Wire bonding is depreciated, U.S.-available and ~10x cheaper per die than TSV stacking; 64 dies per package is ~10x+ capacity per footprint vs 4-8-die DDR packages.

title: Ge-Sn: group-IV emitters beam data vertically through HBM dies
idea: Grow GeSn light emitters at ~2 um wavelength (where silicon is transparent) and matching GeSn photodiodes on each core die so bit lanes pass optically straight through the thinned stack, dropping signal TSVs; the base die converts to the unchanged HBM interface.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): optical vertical channels avoid TSV keep-out and alignment loss while staying CMOS-compatible; speculative ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Transfer-print thin memory membranes, then wire them lithographically
idea: Reverse bond-then-connect: undercut-release memory chiplets into <10 um membranes, pick them with a PDMS stamp onto the logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and pattern vias and copper across both with ordinary lithography, giving a monolithic-like 2-3 um-pitch connection with no bumps.
why: Fact 5: interconnect density ~10x microbumps at ~0.05 pJ/bit, using university-standard transfer printing, spin coating and plating.

title: Spin-wave buses carry data between MRAM banks without charge
idea: Eliminate charge-carrying wires between NV banks: CoFeB or YIG magnonic waveguides move data as spin-wave phase from one bank's MTJ transducers to others, with interference-based fan-out to many banks at once.
why: Inter-bank copies and broadcasts at ~aJ-fJ per bit with no Joule heating in wires.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs with one top-metal mask
idea: Po: dies talk by magnetism. One added thick top-metal mask forms coil arrays on each DRAM die; dies are stacked face-to-back with no TSVs, data crosses by near-field inductive coupling through the thinned silicon, and power arrives by edge wire bonds.
why: Removes TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal steps (HBM TSV tax) for a single mask; ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vertical links.

title: Spare-die HBM stacks with base-die crossbar remapping
idea: Stack yield compounds as y^N, so 12 dies at 98% bond yield gives ~78%. Build 13-high stacks whose base die holds a channel crossbar that remaps any failed die to the spare, plus spare TSV lanes rerouted at runtime without fuses.
why: Turns compounding yield into binomial 12-of-13 yield, recovering most of HBM's 20-30% yield loss for ~8% extra silicon (fact 6).

title: Orthogonal-access memory reads rows or columns, killing transposes
idea: Eliminate transpose and relayout copies: each cell in a dedicated tile gets two access devices on orthogonal wordline/bitline pairs (dual-port 2T gain cell), so a weight tile is read row-major in the forward pass and column-major in the backward pass without being moved.
why: Transposes and layout shuffles cost an extra read+write of tensors (~10-20% of training traffic); a small dual-port region at ~1.5x cell area removes that traffic.

title: Transpose in the base die: return columns, not rows
idea: Rearrange data order at the stack boundary: a small SRAM corner-turn buffer in the HBM base die gathers strided elements (e.g. one head's slice across many tokens of a KV cache) from open rows in many banks and packs them into dense column-major bursts, so the link carries only the bytes requested.
why: Overfetch and link energy (facts 5, 8): for strided or sparse access, link bytes and pJ fall 2-8x because waste is discarded on-stack, millimetres from the array, instead of after crossing the PHY.

title: Undiced DRAM tiles stitched across scribe lanes by one mask
idea: Po: the wafer is never diced. Leave 4x4 groups of DRAM dies attached; one added top-metal mask stitches a wide shared bus across the scribe lanes to a central bond field where a processor chiplet is bonded face-to-face.
why: Removes interposer, microbumps and per-die packaging for a 16-die memory tile; capacity per package rises 4x at low pJ/bit.

title: Open tall-stack die standard turns memory dies into auctioned commodity
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. A JEDEC-style open spec fixes die size, thickness, pad maps and test interface for stackable DRAM dies so any vendor's dies drop into 32-64-high stacks; buyers reverse-auction dies and independent stackers compete separately.
why: Unbundling die-making from stacking lets tall stacks use the cheapest qualifying dies and opens many stacking houses (including U.S.), holding price flat at 10x dies per package.

title: Diode-laser photoreduction writes copper redistribution lines directly
idea: Combine laser direct imaging with metal deposition: coat a copper-formate/amine complex film, scan a 405 nm GaN diode-laser array to photothermally reduce it into 2-5 um Cu lines, rinse unexposed film and electroless-thicken. No photoresist, no excimer scanner (ArF/KrF need neon) and no argon-sputtered seed.
why: Capital and rare-gas intensity of RDL: maskless one-step RDL layers at ~50% lower cost using commodity GaN lasers, fully U.S. manufacturable.

title: Memory retention energy metric in data-center efficiency codes
idea: Ideal: refresh waste is visible and priced. Closest achievable: add a standardized 'retention energy per stored GB-hour' metric, read from DRAM REF counters, to federal data-center efficiency reporting and procurement alongside PUE, with procurement preference for systems that reach zero refresh on declared workloads.
why: Creates market pull for zero-refresh architectures, since refresh is 16-33% of idle DRAM power and roughly 1-3% of IT energy; a cheap policy lever.

title: Micro-LED imaging-fiber links move HBM a meter from the accelerator
idea: Scale HBM's parallelism into optics: a 2D array of hundreds of micro-LEDs and photodiodes couples into a coherent imaging fiber bundle, each pixel a 2-4 Gb/s lane, so a stack can sit a meter away at HBM-class width with no lasers or SerDes.
why: Frees accelerator beachfront (fact 6) and enables pooled HBM at ~1 pJ/bit (fact 5) with memory cooled separately from the GPU.

title: Layer-major execution turns all memory traffic into hard-drive streams
idea: Weight bytes per token equal W/B for batch B, and random access disappears if you run one layer over an entire corpus before the next. For offline workloads (embedding, synthetic data, evaluation), stream weights and the corpus's activations layer by layer from striped HDD/NAND arrays, with DRAM only as small staging.
why: Working storage at HDD/NAND cost ($0.015-0.05/GB, >100x cheaper); trades latency completely (hours-scale jobs).

title: Acoustic delay-line revival: AlN gigahertz ultrasound bus through the stack
idea: Revive the delay line's acoustic signaling: sputtered AlN transducers (not PVDF fluoropolymer piezo) launch 5-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses that travel vertically through bonded silicon tiers to receivers on every die, forming a broadcast command/address and refresh-control bus.
why: Constraint: AlN and direct silicon bonding need no fluorinated films or TSVs; removes the C/A TSV bundle (~10-20% of TSVs) and gives free broadcast to all tiers at a few Gb/s per transducer.

title: Data over the power network inside the HBM stack
idea: Rearrange power and signal roles: superimpose low-amplitude, high-frequency data on the many power/ground TSVs (which outnumber signal TSVs) using AC coupling and band separation above the PDN resonance, turning idle PDN capacity into extra channels.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): up to 30-50% more effective I/O with no added TSVs; the risk is PDN noise coupling into the array.

title: Bond-pad interleaving makes 1% dead hybrid bonds correctable
idea: Shift the error budget from the cell scale to the bond scale: each codeword's bits are spread across many hybrid-bond pads, so a pad lost to a particle or void looks like scattered bit errors that the 1%-tolerant code already fixes. Bonding then runs with relaxed cleanliness and planarity and no spare-pad repair.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% (fact 6); defect-tolerant bonding recovers most of it and permits cheaper bonders and less cleanroom.

title: Tuning fork: resonant LC clocking for low-power memory PHY
idea: Like a tuning fork ringing at its natural frequency: on-die LC tanks resonate the forwarded clock distribution of a memory PHY, recycling clock charge instead of burning it, demonstrated on one ~$150k MPW shuttle.
why: Clocking is often 30-40% of PHY power; 20-30% lower interface pJ/bit.

title: Interposer that is itself a capacity-tier DRAM
idea: Po: the interposer is the memory. Fabricate the ~2,500 mm2 2.5D silicon interposer, today passive wiring, on a mature trench-capacitor DRAM node so the silicon under and between GPU and HBM becomes a slower but very near capacity tier of several GB, wired to the GPU through the interposer's own dense metal.
why: Turns wasted interposer silicon into bits at mature-node cost per bit with no TSV tax; adds ~4-16 GB per package at <1 pJ/bit with no new EUV capital.

title: Content-addressed memory fabric stores each identical page once
idea: Across a datacenter, KV-cache prefixes, system prompts, libraries and weights repeat thousands of times. A CXL switch hashes 4 KB pages on write, keeps each unique page once in a pooled DRAM/NAND backend, and hands hosts copy-on-write pointers, with a prefix-trie index for KV caches.
why: Shared-prefix chat serving can dedup 10-100x, so effective cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades write latency and isolation complexity.

title: Capillarity: water-droplet self-alignment speeds die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Pattern hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surrounds, dispense a nanoliter water droplet, and drop DRAM dies coarsely; surface tension pulls each die to <200 nm alignment before direct bonding, so placement tools run 10x faster at coarse accuracy.
why: HBM assembly capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): hybrid bonders are slow and costly; capillary alignment cuts bonder capex per stack.

title: No-TSV shingled staircase stack with printed edge ramps
idea: Eliminate TSVs: offset each DRAM die ~200 um like roof shingles so every die exposes a ledge of fine-pitch pads, then plate or aerosol-jet-print copper 'ramps' down the stairs to the base die at 10-20 um pitch, using several ledge rows for a 1024-bit bus. No via etch, no via reveal, no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% yield loss): recovers the ~10-15% of die area spent on TSV arrays and keep-out, removes via-reveal steps and their yield loss; claimed ~20-30% lower HBM cost/bit.

title: Base-die KV-cache codec stores ten contexts in one's space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. The HBM base die compresses KV-cache blocks on write (per-channel 2-bit quantization, residual low-rank sketch, entropy-coded outliers) and decompresses on read at line rate, transparent to the GPU kernels.
why: KV cache dominates LLM serving memory; ~8-10x compression inside the module raises effective bits per purchased bit about 10x.

title: Origami stack: one thinned die folded into eight layers
idea: Po: chips are folded, not stacked. Fabricate eight DRAM arrays on one reticle-stitched strip, thin it to ~15 um with polyimide-backed hinge zones carrying continuous metal, and fold it accordion-style so every inter-layer link is an ordinary on-die wire running through a fold.
why: No TSVs and no bonding steps, so stack yield loss from TSV/bond defects disappears; thousands of fold wires at 2 um pitch give HBM-class width.
